what.heading: What this console is
what.clients: This service exists to exercise clients, and the pages here exist to exercise the parts of a client that only show themselves when something changes underneath it: what happens when a token it holds stops being valid, and what happens when a token it reads grows a claim it was not expecting.
what.derived: Every page in the sidebar is below, in the sidebar's own order and grouping, because this list is DERIVED from the same table the sidebar is drawn from. A page cannot be added to this console and left out of here; one added without a description says so on its own row rather than going quietly.
not.heading: What it deliberately does not do
not.intro: Worth knowing before looking for a control that is not here. This list is shown in development mode only, because almost all of it is about what development mode does not check.
not.invalidate: It does not invalidate a SAML assertion or a Kerberos ticket. It counts them, it lists them on the tokens page beside the JWTs, and it says when each expires — but neither has a revocation mechanism a relying party consults. A SAML assertion is valid because its signature verifies and its Conditions hold, and a Kerberos ticket because the service it names can decrypt it; nothing about this service is asked in either case. A button claiming to revoke one would change a number here and nothing at all out there, which is why those rows carry a dash and the reason for it. The same is true one family further out: an X509-SVID already handed to a workload keeps working until it expires, and banning a SPIFFE identity records who may still be ISSUED one, which is a different claim. A verifiable credential is not on this list: its status list is how one is revoked.
not.endSessionA: It does not deliver front-channel logout. It does end sign-on sessions:
not.endSessionB: ends one through the same function every sign-out uses, and so does
not.endSessionC: , without a console role. A front-channel notification is an iframe in the signed-out person's own browser, and this console is not that browser. Back-channel Logout Tokens need no browser, and this service sends them whichever door ended the session.
not.keepTokens: It does not keep the tokens themselves, only their claims. A page listing a thousand live bearer credentials in a form a browser will render is a page that leaks them, and the jti is all any button here needs. One configured field is held back for the same reason and no stronger one: a federation relationship's fedClientSecret is this service's own credential AT a real foreign service, so it is never printed here and never reaches the audit log — an ldapsearch shows it anyway, and this console not being a second way to read it is not a security boundary.
not.restart: NOTHING THIS SERVICE MINTS SURVIVES A RESTART, and a restart is not a reload. The counters, the token and artifact registries, the audit ring, the sessions, the authorization codes and the Kerberos tickets are all in memory, and the signing key is REGENERATED on every start — so a token issued by the previous process no longer verifies against the published JWKS. That is deliberate rather than a limitation, and it is what makes the rest of it impossible: a statistics file, or a stored token, that outlived the key it was signed under would be worse than none.
not.surviveOn: THREE THINGS DO SURVIVE on this process, because persistence.mode is {mode}: the embedded directory — which is also the applications registry, the federation register and the SPIFFE registry — the trust realm registry, and the settings changed on these pages. Those are the things somebody TYPED.
not.surviveOff: THREE THINGS CAN BE MADE TO SURVIVE and are not on this process — the embedded directory, the trust realms and the settings changed here.
not.rememberA: It does not remember everything, either. The token, artifact and user registries and the audit ring are CAPPED and drop their oldest rows — and each says how many it dropped rather than pretending they were never there:
not.rememberB: , and one collapsed row for the paths that matched no route. A count that grew without limit would be one a scanner inventing URLs could exhaust.
not.password: It checks no password — not even at its own door. Signing in to this console proves that somebody typed a name that holds one of two roles, and nothing verifies that it is them. The roles are ordinary directory groups, so an ldapmodify or a SCIM PATCH grants them too. Until the realm's bootstrap administrator first signs in, anybody who signs in holds both while admin.openWhenEmpty is on. None of this makes this port safe to expose.
not.enforceA: It enforces little, and widening is what most of these pages do. RFC 9700 mode, which OAuth 2.1 mode implies, is what makes this service refuse what it would otherwise accept, and it is off unless
not.enforceB: turn it on. Three surfaces still ask for a credential —
not.enforceC: , the SPIRE Server API and this console. None of them can be turned off. Development mode changes how much of what they ask for is checked, and none of them checks a password.
not.enforceD: is the one refusal that is not a mode and cannot be switched off, because at an assertion consumer service there is no permissive answer available.
not.delegateA: It does not refuse a delegation that the delegation policy would refuse.
not.delegateB: records every act. At WS-Trust's OnBehalfOf and ActAs and at RFC 8693 token exchange the policy is still asked, and a refusal is written on the act's row as “would have been refused”. Product mode enforces it.
not.attestA: It does not attest a caller of the SPIFFE Workload API over TCP. There is no peer process to ask, so the caller is known by its transport, the endpoint it reached and its source address. In development mode
not.attestB: also lets a registration entry select its workload on nothing that identifies one. The Workload API authenticates nobody because its specification says it MUST NOT, so what a caller lacks there is attestation rather than authentication.
not.deleteA: It deletes CONFIGURATION and never a person. An authorization server, a SPIFFE registration entry, an attested agent's record and a federation relationship can all be removed here. A PERSON cannot be: somebody can be created on
not.deleteB: ahead of their first sign-in and a SPIFFE identity can be banned so that no further SVID is issued to it, but no control in this console deletes an entry under ou=users. One name is ONE entry however that name authenticated, which is the property most of these pages are reading.
not.deleteC: is the exception and it is a whole protocol rather than a button — a
not.deleteD: really does remove the entry, while its active: false DISABLES the account (2026-09-17), which is the same act as Disable on a person's page.
not.oneRealm: It shows ONE trust realm at a time, and it writes the one it is read in. Every page here reports the realm in the path it was reached by, and the switcher above the nav is how you leave it — so a setting saved on any of these pages changes that realm and no other. A realm has administrators of its own since 2026-09-14: the two role groups in its own directory, confined to that realm, while the default realm's two groups remain the service administrators over every realm. A realm administrator does not see the pages about the whole process, and is refused them if they ask.
test.heading: Reading it from a test
test.noteA: Every page above is drawn from an operation of the management API, and every form is sent to one, so a test reads and writes the same answers with no browser. A call presents an access token this service issued for the API, with admin:read for a read and admin:write for a change. A call without one gets 401 with a JSON body, never a redirect to a sign-in screen. Every operation is listed at
test.noteB: , and in development mode adminApi.authRequired off opens the API to any caller. A few to start with:
test.groups: — the second carries every attribute of that group and every member resolved.
test.users: — the second carries sessions, each with the tokens issued on it, plus the tokens that belong to no session and the artifacts
test.tokens: — the reply carries page, pages and matched, so walking the whole list needs no guess about where it ends. Every paged list here answers the same three fields, so one walker serves all of them.
test.metadata: — every endpoint this process registered, which is the list to check a client's assumptions against rather than this page.
test.map: for the graph, and ?format=svg for the drawing alone — the one page here with a fourth shape.
undescribed: this page has no description in SECTIONS. It was added to the nav and not described here; the list you are reading is derived from that table, so this row is the report rather than a gap.
